pending_items.title: Residents of Jordan Valley vow to remain after Israeli bulldozers raze homes
pending_items.content:
The latest Israeli attempt to expel the Palestinian residents of Khirbet Samra, located in the northern Jordan Valley of the occupied West Bank, resulted in the demolition of all structures in the community on Sunday.

The demolition spared nothing, not even livestock troughs, residents told Middle East Eye.

The Israeli army went further, burying the debris to ensure the residents could not salvage or reuse any of it.

Currently, the remaining residents of Khirbet Samra are living in tents provided by human rights organisations. Yet, despite everything, they say they are determined to stay.

Dhiab Daraghmeh, a resident, said that more than 15 structures were demolished, including family homes, sheep pens, shelters for young livestock, and storage areas for fodder and hay.

He said that the Israeli army arrived unexpectedly on Sunday, accompanied by bulldozers, as the residents were caught off guard, having received no prior notice.

The Israelis gave them only ten minutes to retrieve some of their belongings from their homes. This brief window allowed them to save only a few minor items.

Almost everything else was destroyed: furniture, kitchenware, gas cylinders, refrigerators, livestock troughs, as well as bathrooms, water tanks, solar panels, and fodder storage units.

'For three days, we have been living without shelter, enduring cold nights and high daytime temperatures'

Residents now face a grim future. With winter approaching and no shelter available, families are forced to sleep in the open, while their belongings and essential supplies are left exposed to the sun and rain.

"For three days, we have been living without shelter, enduring cold nights and high daytime temperatures. We are also deeply concerned for our newborn lambs, which cannot survive in these conditions," said Daraghmeh.

The families’ needs go beyond food and humanitarian aid; primarily, they seek the right to remain on their land, to rebuild what the Israeli bulldozers destroyed and to secure protection for themselves and their livestock against the winter elements.

The demolitions are part of a long-standing pattern of attacks by Israeli settlers, a campaign that has persisted for years to displace the local population, with several communities targeted across the northern Jordan Valley.

The assaults have been ongoing since 2017 and have taken various forms, including the killing of livestock and the destruction of residents' property, actions that, three months ago, forced more than half of the community’s residents to leave and relocate to the city of Tubas.

"On June 11, 2025, settlers killed about 50 of my sheep, just one of the incidents in which I have suffered significant losses. Yet, these attacks have not driven the families to leave the area," Dhiyab added.

The residents of Khirbet Samra maintain their right to remain in the community as the land is owned by the families, inherited from their ancestors.

"My grandfather lived in this area before 1977. The family resided in various locations throughout the region before Israeli harassment, along with claims that certain lands were 'nature reserves' or 'military zones', forced them to relocate to the community’s current site," he said.

Only 21 people remain in the community, after repeated attacks by settlers that, months earlier, forced more than 24 others to leave and effectively turned the small community into an open-air prison.

Another resident, Ayman Daraghmeh, said that they had asked the soldiers for permission to access drinking water, but the request was denied shortly before the bulldozers arrived to demolish the structures.

Among the items destroyed by the bulldozers was a tree that had been planted about 16 years ago.

Once a tiny sapling, it had grown over the years to become an integral part of the family’s life and their daily memories.

"I brought it here as a small sapling about 16 years ago; my children and I used to love sitting beneath it. This tree grew up alongside us, and now they have demolished everything around it," Daraghmeh said.

He said that approximately ten tons of barley were buried under the rubble, along with quantities of animal feed and the structures used to store it.

Daraghmeh estimated the material losses for the feeding troughs alone at approximately 1,500 shekels ($451) each.

“The near-daily actions of settlers have confined us to a narrow area, making us feel as though we are living in a prison, unable to move freely beyond the small patch of land where we reside,” he said.

In its humanitarian report issued on 18 November 2026, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said that approximately 6,800 Palestinians, including more than 3,200 children, have been displaced since the beginning of 2023 due to settler attacks and associated restrictions on land access.

This displacement has affected 137 Palestinian communities, 51 of which have been completely emptied of their inhabitants.

In 2026 alone, 2,894 Palestinians were displaced as a result of settler attacks and related access restrictions. The Jordan Valley accounted for 44 percent of all displacements linked to settler attacks and access restrictions during 2026.

Mahdi Daraghmeh, head of the Al-Maleh and Bedouin Communities Council, said that for the past two years, the community has faced escalating attacks by settlers that intensified following the establishment of a nearby settler outpost.

'Settlers deliberately bring their own livestock onto these lands and keep them there, effectively preventing the residents from utilizing the area'

He told MEE that settlers break into their homes, often calling in army and police forces, who sometimes detain the residents.

The assaults extended to seizing the natural resources upon which the residents depend for their livelihoods.

Settlers have taken control of water wells near the community, blocking families from accessing or using them. They have also seized vast areas of grazing land, preventing residents from taking their livestock out to pasture.

This pressure has further extended to rain-fed agricultural lands that families traditionally cultivated on a seasonal basis, using them for both grazing and harvesting crops.

“Settlers deliberately bring their own livestock onto these lands and keep them there, effectively preventing the residents from utilising the area,” he said.

According to Draghmeh, the Israeli army continues to maintain a daily presence in the community, threatening residents against constructing any new facilities and demanding that they leave the area.

"The residents of Khirbet Samra rely primarily on livestock farming for their livelihood. Consequently, the seizure of grazing lands and water wells along with the destruction of animal pens and fodder storage poses a direct threat to their ability to continue living in the region," he added.

According to local Palestinians, the happenings in Khirbet Samra are part of a broader pattern of attacks and encirclement targeting Bedouin communities in the northern Jordan Valley.

According to Draghmeh, six Bedouin communities have been completely depopulated, with approximately 200 families displaced in the last two years.

pending_items.title: Israel unity government talks stall: What happens now?
pending_items.content:
The future of Israel’s government remains unclear following October elections that produced no clear winner.

The leader of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, and his main rival, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, have been convening for rounds of talks in a bid to establish a “unity government”.

But the talks ended on Sunday without a conclusive deal, with the two parties announcing that a “follow-up” meeting will be held soon.

So, what is the latest on the talks? And what happens if they fail to reach an agreement?

Following the October 27 general election, Israeli President Isaac Herzog held consultations with political parties to decide who he would appoint to form a government after neither side secured a majority. Eisenkot and his presumed partners won 48 seats between them, while Netanyahu’s alliance won 53.

Some 67 lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, endorsed Eisenkot to form the next government, while only 46 backed Netanyahu.

In November, Eisenkot was instructed by Israel’s president to form a new government by December 6, with a deadline that can be extended by 14 days.

In order to form a government, one party, alliance or coalition requires a minimum 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. This means Eisenkot must ally with other parties or lawmakers to make up the seat numbers.

Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats in the election. But Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with them, which would have given him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.

He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote.

Until this week, Eisenkot had struck firm coalition deals with only the Democrats and Yisrael Beiteinu, bringing his total to 36 seats out of a potential 48 – still far from any majority.

Eisenkot has, therefore, been talking to Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party in hopes of establishing a unity government , but Likud wants a rotation deal that would go against Eisenkot’s promise to replace Netanyahu.

The talks have caused other complications as well. The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot this week in protest at the prospect of Netanyahu’s party remaining in government.

On Tuesday, the Yashar party announced that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with the Yisrael Beiteinu party, after meeting with leader Avigdor Lieberman, marking the first confirmed alliance since the election.

Israeli media also reported on Friday that Netanyahu is “preparing” to announce that he is willing to serve second in a prime minister rotation with Eisenkot under a unity government deal.

Israel’s public broadcaster Kan reported that the offer had already been proposed unofficially, so Likud could assume “plausible deniability”, as the party remains conflicted on the terms of the offer.

The rotation deal would mean that Eisenkot would serve for the first two years as prime minister, and Netanyahu would serve the final two years.

But in a statement on Friday, Eisenkot accused the Likud party of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections. He claimed that Likud was “unwilling to compromise, and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table”.

Eisenkot said the two sides are “approaching a moment of decision”, but the question is “whether Likud will engage in serious negotiations and commit to a partnership that requires compromise or keep up appearances and continue to stall”.

Meanwhile, Eisenkot is grappling with division among his own side as the options of forging alliances with ultra-Orthodox parties or the Arab-majority parties, who are willing to back him, have proved controversial.

The Arab-led parties could give Yashar 19 seats, but Lieberman has said he will not support any government that includes those parties.

Eisenkot said Likud’s negotiating team had refused to meet more frequently over the past two weeks. The two sides have met five times.

He added that their team was uncooperative and had rejected three proposals, including one for a state inquiry into the “failures” of October 7, the removal of “extremists” from government and a law making military or national service mandatory for all.

Instead, Eisenkot claimed that Likud proposed “the worst” proposal for a unity government with “the same government, the same partners, no change, no conscription law”.

Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s strategy is to “run down the clock until the mandate expires”, attempting to “drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government”.

“I do not intend to cooperate with such a charade,” he added.

One of Eisenkot’s options is to reach a deal with the country’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas. But if talks with them fail, analysts say Eisenkot could ask his allies to choose between keeping Netanyahu in office or accepting support from the Arab-led parties.

The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties, holds 11 seats in the Knesset, while Ra’am holds eight.

Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator and president of the US/Middle East Project, told Al Jazeera that if this were to happen, Eisenkot could tell his allies to “form a government for a few months, just to get Bibi [Netanyahu] out of power and prepare for new elections”.

Analysts say that if Eisenkot reaches his deadline of December 6 to form a government without a decision, Israeli President Herzog could assign the task to another member of the Knesset, including Netanyahu, and give them a 28-day period to form a government with no extensions.

If still no government is formed, Israel could move towards a new round of elections, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister until a government is formed.

This happened in 2019, after the April election, when Netanyahu was unable to form a government. As a result, the Knesset was dissolved and a second election took place in September that year. Again, no majority was reached, leading to a third vote in March 2020. A government was finally formed later that month when Netanyahu struck a unity government deal with Benny Gantz’s Blue and White alliance.

pending_items.title: As Spain votes, what could change for Europe?
pending_items.content:
Walking through the halls of the European institutions in Brussels these days, it feels as if people are whispering about the end of an era. What happens when one of the most vocal leaders of Europe's center left is no longer at the table?

Pedro Sanchez is one of the few social democratic prime ministers left in the European Union, and Spain is the largest member state still led by one. That's why this election raises questions that go beyond who governs in Madrid .

After more than eight years in office Sanchez called a snap election at the beginning of October, three days after parliament rejected two emergency decrees aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis. Anger over soaring housing costs has brought protesters onto the streets nationwide this year .

Sanchez's minority government was already under pressure over its handling of the summer migration crisis in Ceuta and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife have denied.

Polls on Monday predicted a tight race, putting the conservative People's Party (PP) at around 32% and the Socialists led by Sanchez at 31%.

With the right-wing populist Vox party in third place at around 17%, the polling projected an absolute majority for the PP and Vox combined. The two parties would still have to decide whether they want to govern together.

A change of government in Madrid would cost Europe's center left one of its most influential voices , Javier Carbonell, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre in Brussels, told DW. "This voice might now be silenced."

Carbonell said three positions have set Sanchez apart: his willingness to challenge US President Donald Trump , his support for Palestinian statehood and his defense of immigration into Europe. Sanchez has been one of the few EU leaders who have continued to argue that migrant workers help fill labor shortages, support an aging Spanish and European population and sustain growth .

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier this year, his government opened a program to grant legal status to eligible migrants already living in Spain. It received more than 1 million applications. Spain's economy grew by 2.6% last year, nearly double the eurozone average, and the government expects GDP to grow by 2.6% this year and 2.2% in 2027.

The conservative PP has campaigned for tighter immigration controls while keeping routes open for workers in sectors facing shortages. Vox wants sharper cuts to immigration, more deportations and an end to regularization for new arrivals. It also wants Spanish citizens to get priority for subsidized housing and other social benefits.

This stance is nothing new at the European level . "With a PP-Vox government, Spain would join the general European trend towards an anti-immigration policy," said Carbonell, adding that he could see Madrid moving closer to countries pushing for tougher return policies. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands are already in talks with Rwanda about setting up a hub for people whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Camino Mortera-Martinez, an associate fellow at the Centre for European Reform, agrees that a shift in Madrid would reinforce a trend already underway in Europe . "This anti-migration tendency doesn't come from European leaders, but from voters," she told DW.

Another domain where Spain could potentially change course and influence its European neighbors concerns its defense policies. Spain raised defense spending from 1.24% of GDP in 2024 to 2% in 2025, reaching NATO's previous benchmark.

Nevertheless, Sanchez has pushed back against the alliance's new annual target of 5% of GDP by 2035 , which includes both military spending and broader security investments. He has argued that Spain could meet its NATO capability commitments by spending around 2.1% of GDP.

Both the PP and Vox favor higher defense investment but leave the exact figure open in their election programs. "They have a voting base that has no problem to increase defense spending, contrary to Sanchez," said Mortera-Martinez.

Mortera-Martinez also expects a change in Spain's approach to the Middle East , should Sanchez lose the election.

"The current government has been at the forefront of defending the last bastions of international and public law," she said.

Spain formally recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. Sanchez has accused European leaders of applying double standards by rallying behind Ukraine against Russia's invasion, while failing to defend international law with the same resolve in the Middle East. In April, he pushed to suspend the EU's agreement with Israel, which makes respect for human rights an essential part of the relationship.

Carbonell, too, believes a new conservative government would be less vocal in its support for the Palestinians. "Sanchez was able to influence people on the subject matter, moving the consensus a bit more towards pro-Palestine," he said.

If Sanchez comes up short on Sunday, Europe's social democrats would lose their strongest foothold among the EU's largest countries. But, said Carbonell, a defeat in Spain could reignite a debate across the European center left about how to win back voters and stay politically relevant elsewhere.
